newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU to get Credit Lyonnais plan by end July - source.
newsitem.headline: EU to get Credit Lyonnais plan by end July - source.

text.p: France's new leftist government should give the European Union a plan by the end of this month that is likely to pave the way for the sale of state-owned bank Credit Lyonnais, a well-informed source said on Monday.
The restructuring plan, involving disposal of most of the bank's European assets outside France in exchange for approval of state aid, could be forwarded before the end of the week.
The EU's executive body, the European Commission, is expected to insist on a French commitment to sell the bank before giving its approval.

The source said the long-awaited plan "has not been significantly altered" from one which the previous conservative government drafted before being ousted from power in an election seven weeks ago by the Socialist-led coalition.
The Socialists campaigned on a pledge to halt state sell-offs but have since retreated on that commitment.
The government announced last Friday it would not block the privatisation planned by its predecesssors of money-losing insurer GAN and its profitable banking arm CIC.

The announcement followed Prime Minister Lionel Jospin questioning the state's role in bailing out financial institutions which have cost the state billions of francs. He pledged not to allow ideology to stand in the way of national interest.
Credit Lyonnais has staged a strong recovery from an ill-fated expansion spree carried out when the Socialists were previously in power and which nearly resulted in its collapse.
The final tally from its misadventures, which led to a series of state bailouts, is seen at around 170 billion francs ($28.1 billion).
Credit Lyonnais urgently needs the Commission's approval for a decision by the previous government to neutralise the cost of a cheap loan granted by the bank under a 1995 state rescue.
The loan was given by the bank to finance the spinoff of its bad assets into a separate holding company.
Without the approval, its performance would be badly hit as the cost of the loan is estimated at three billion francs which would wipe out its expected 1997 net profit of around 1.5 billion francs.

The former government said it might sell the bank this year. Bank chairman Jean Peyrelevade, who enjoys close links with the Socialists, said last month he believed the new government would privatise the bank but that the sale would not take place before the end of 1998.
"We need to be sufficiently prosperous which is not yet the case," he told the regional newspaper La Provence.

He said the bank would need less than five billion francs in extra state funds to boost its balance sheet to make it saleable. But the proceeds from selling the bank, 80 percent state-owned, would total 20 to 25 billion francs, he said.

Meanwhile, the bank was expected to sign a deal this week to sell its majority stake in Italian bank Credito Bergamasco (Creberg) to Italy's Banco Popolare di Verona as part of its asset disposal drive, another source said.
Once briefly the world's largest bank outside Japan, Credit Lyonnais intends to limit its retail banking to France and focus on wholesale and capital market operations elsewhere.
